The Data

About the Dataset

We use the Spotify Top Songs dataset, which includes popular tracks from 2010 to 2019. Each song has audio features and basic metadata.

The dataset combines categorical variables like artist, genre, and year with numerical features like energy, danceability, valence, acousticness, and popularity. It enables us to compare songs, track changes over time, and explore relationships between features.

Project Goals

What We Aimed to Do

  • →To analyze the Spotify Top Songs dataset to understand patterns in popular music from 2010 to 2019
  • →To examine how song characteristics vary over time, genres, and artists
  • →To explore how key audio features relate to song popularity
  • →To present these findings in an interactive dashboard that makes the results easy to explore and understand

Research Questions

What We Set Out to Answer

01
How do song characteristics change over time?
We compare features like energy, danceability, and acousticness from 2010 to 2019 and identify the year with the highest average danceability.
02
How do audio feature patterns differ across genres?
We compare genres using energy, acousticness, danceability, and valence to see if distinct musical patterns emerge.
03
What similarities and differences appear across artists?
We examine the artists who appear most often in the dataset and compare their musical profiles.
04
How do audio features relate to popularity?
We explore whether features like danceability, energy, and valence are linked to popularity and which has the strongest relationship.

Key Findings

What the Data Reveals

Average danceability rose from 64.5 in 2010 to 69.7 in 2019, showing a steady upward trend, particularly in later years.

Neo mellow stands out for acousticness
Among the top 10 genres, neo mellow has the highest relative acousticness, making it distinct from more energetic genres like big room and boy band.

Danceability shows the strongest link to popularity
Among the audio features, danceability has the strongest positive relationship with popularity (r = 0.116), while energy shows a slight negative relationship.

Key Insights

What the Charts Show

Each chart addresses one of our research questions. Below is a guide to what each chart shows and what insights users can take away.

Average Danceability by Year

The average danceability of songs went up over the decade, starting at around 64.5 in 2010 and reaching almost 70 by 2019. There was a drop in the middle of the decade, but danceability rose steadily again after 2016.

Relative Audio Feature Profiles by Genre

Each genre has its own feature pattern rather than sharing a single sound profile. For example, neo mellow is more acoustic and has lower energy. Boy band and big room have higher energy and valence.

Danceability and Popularity

There is a small positive connection between danceability and popularity, so songs that are easier to dance to tend to be a little more popular. However, the data show that danceability alone does not strongly predict how popular a song will be.

Top 10 Artists by Number of Songs

Katy Perry shows up the most in the dataset, with Justin Bieber, Rihanna, and Maroon 5 close behind. This means a few artists were on the charts often and had a big presence during these years.

Top 10 Genres by Average Popularity

A small group of genres have the highest average popularity scores. Escape room ranks first, with brostep and alternative r&b close behind. The top genres have similar scores, so several styles were equally popular.

Chart Guide

How to Read the Dashboard

Each chart in the dashboard is interactive. Below is a guide to what each chart shows, how to use its interactive features, and why those features add value.

Research Question Addressed

"How does the distribution of a selected audio feature in one chosen year compare with the overall distribution across all songs from 2010 to 2019?"

How the Chart is Interactive

The chart has two dropdowns. One lets users choose an audio feature to visualize, such as danceability, energy, valence, acousticness, or popularity. The other lets them select a year from 2010 to 2019. The visualization updates to show two side-by-side boxplots: one for all years and one for the selected year. Hovering over a boxplot reveals detailed summary statistics, including median, Q1, Q3, IQR, whisker values, and outlier count. The chart also includes an annotation comparing the selected-year median with the overall median.

Why This Interactivity Adds Value

This interactivity makes the chart more useful than a static boxplot, as users are not limited to a single feature or year. They can test different comparisons and see how the distribution shape changes by feature and time period. The hover statistics provide precise values, making the boxplot easier to interpret. The median comparison annotation helps users quickly see whether the selected year is above or below the overall pattern.

Research Question Addressed

"How do musical feature patterns differ across genres, and which genres stand out in terms of acousticness, danceability, energy, and valence?"

How the Chart is Interactive

The chart includes feature checkboxes that let users turn individual audio features on or off, so they can focus on the features they want to compare. It also has a sorting dropdown that reorders genres by a selected feature. A highlight-genre dropdown lets users emphasize one genre while keeping others visible for comparison. Hovering over any cell reveals the exact genre, feature, and relative value shown by the color.

Why This Interactivity Adds Value

These interactions make the heatmap more useful than a static view because users can adapt it to the comparisons they care about. The feature toggles reduce clutter. The sorting control reveals ranking patterns more clearly. The highlight dropdown helps users focus on one genre without losing context. The hover details make the color scale easier to interpret by providing exact values, allowing users to move from broad visual patterns to precise comparisons.

Research Question Addressed

"Which genres have the highest average popularity, and how do the most popular genres compare with one another?"

How the Chart is Interactive

The chart has dropdown menus for both the x-axis and y-axis, letting users choose which audio features to compare, such as danceability, energy, valence, acousticness, or popularity. It also has a Top N selector to control how many genres are displayed and a highlight-genre dropdown to focus on one genre while keeping the rest visible. Hovering over a bubble reveals detailed information, including genre name, average popularity, song count, and exact values for the selected axes. Bubble size shows the number of songs in that genre, while color shows average popularity.

Why This Interactivity Adds Value

These interactions make the chart more useful than a static genre comparison, as users can explore how popular genres compare in different ways. The axis selectors let them test whether the same genres stand out across different feature combinations. The Top N control keeps the chart readable. The highlight dropdown makes it easier to track one genre without losing the overall pattern. The hover details add precision by showing exact values, letting users move from broad visual clusters to detailed comparisons.

Research Question Addressed

"How do audio features relate to popularity, and which feature shows the strongest relationship with popular songs?"

How the Chart is Interactive

The chart includes a feature dropdown that lets users switch the x-axis to audio features such as danceability, energy, valence, and acousticness. It also has a year range slider that filters songs to a selected period. When users change the feature or year range, the scatterplot and dashed trend line update automatically along with the displayed correlation value. Hovering over a point reveals song details such as track title, artist, selected feature value, and popularity score.

Why This Interactivity Adds Value

These interactions make the chart more useful than a static scatterplot because users can test multiple hypotheses in the same view. The feature dropdown helps users compare which audio attributes relate more closely to popularity. The year slider shows whether those relationships change across the decade. Hover details add value by connecting each point to a specific song, letting users move from broad patterns to individual examples and outliers.
